items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: Elvin Jones group makes use of a lot of youngsters such as Nicholas Payton

ctx.x: Could you name a couple of those groups?

Young groups, you know like Terrance Blanchard, of course the Elvin Jones group makes use of a lot of youngsters such as Nicholas Payton and they even use Coltrane’s son, Ravi Coltrane with Elvin Jones. And of course Vincent Herring, an alto saxophonist, Jesse Davis, another alto saxophonist, Bobby Watson, another alto saxophonist, Roy Hargrove, Chris McBride, Antonio Hart. These are the youngsters that are, that are carrying on authentic jazz. This is not the Basie style, now, I’m talking about small group jazz.…
No, not necessarily doing the Basie thing, but in other words, just putting your thumb on the pulse and saying, are the traditions alive and well?

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: You have your exceptions like the Marsalises and the Terence Blanchards and the Nicholas Paytons and all that crowd that came from New Orleans and are inundating the jazz scene now

ctx.x: Do you have some sense of -- in your view is the music taking on some quality, significantly different quality, because it’s being learned in a different, if you will, a sterile setting as opposed to a setting which is infused with life experience and directly tied to community?

You can check out the number of groups that are out there now. You have your exceptions like the Marsalises and the Terence Blanchards and the Nicholas Paytons and all that crowd that came from New Orleans and are inundating the jazz
scene now, but how many groups do you have like the old Jazz Messengers, like Horace Silver, and Miles, Coltrane, and --
